blocks.text: In Britain, occupational classification is the principal mode of social classification; the social class of a household is determined on the basis of the head of the family.

blocks.caption: Table: Classes 1-6 with categories (Class 1: Professional, managerial and ...; Class 2: Intermediate; Class 3: Skilled, manual, clerical; Class 4: semi-skilled; Class 5: unskilled; Class 6: unemployed).

blocks.text: Dominance and dependence are two essential underlying themes behind the categorical divisions of social classes.
Most psychiatric disorders are more common in lower social classes, with controversial exceptions noted for anorexia, alcohol use and bipolar disorders.

Anorexia: it is debatable whether social class affects true prevalence or whether differential rates reflect variations in help-seeking/referral pattern. The growing consensus is that social classes 1 and 2 are more prevalent in clinical (as opposed to community-based) samples, with no differences across social groups in the distribution of clinical features or in family relationships/constellations; the prodrome (excessive diet consciousness) and onset occur at somewhat younger ages in classes 1/2.

In a clinical psychiatric population anorexia nervosa is the keyed disorder that is more common in the higher social classes (autism, bulimia nervosa, **ADHD** and schizophrenia are the distractors). The explanation says the clinical social-class distribution is consistently weighted toward classes 1/2 and that whether this reflects help-seeking/referral patterns or true prevalence is debated; community studies show no association with social class.

blocks.text: Community studies show the degree of urbanization has a significant impact on the prevalence of anorexia, bulimia and binge eating disorder (Favaro et al., 2003); social class, professional status and education are not associated with an increased risk of reporting an eating disorder in such community samples.

Bipolar disorder: there is overrepresentation of the higher occupational class in probands' brothers and children; families of origin of bipolar probands belong to a higher social class though the patients themselves might be at a lower class. Tsuchiya et al. (2004): higher parental social class, longer paternal education and larger possession of wealth increased bipolar risk in the offspring. It is speculated that 'bipolar genes' may offer survival benefits such as superior creativity or productivity, which uplifts families to higher social status.

Bipolar disorder is the keyed answer for over-representation of the higher social class among probands' brothers and children (Tsuchiya et al. 2004, Danish registers) - anorexia nervosa, alcoholism, depressive disorder and antisocial personality are not keyed. The explanation adds that the probands' family of origin is of higher class even though the patients themselves may be in a lower class.

blocks.text: Suicide: the relationship with social class has not been conclusively established; some authors report higher social class related to higher suicide rates.
Most other studies indicate lower social class is associated with higher suicide rates; among the mentally ill, the higher the social class, the more the risk of suicide (Silverton et al. 2008).

Alcoholism seems to defy social class boundaries. A Swedish conscript study (Hemmingson et al., 1999): intergenerational social mobility associated with health-related factors, but not alcoholism itself, contributes to explaining variation in alcoholism rates between classes. Class-related differences among young adults are heavily influenced by factors established by adolescence. By far a significant influence on alcohol-related harm appears to be public health policy on pricing and sales of alcohol.

In all aspects of health, including life expectancy and infant and maternal mortality, there is a discrepancy between social classes despite the **NHS** having been developed to combat this. It is a question whether low social class leads to poor health or poor health leads to deterioration in social status (as suggested in the Danish bipolar study above); cultural differences among classes (diet, exercise, alcohol intake, awareness of mental health problems and treatments) also need consideration.

blocks.text: The sick role is a concept described by the American sociologist Talcott Parsons.

Under Parsons, **TAKING** **SELF-BLAME** for the illness is the behaviour regarded as abnormal - extending absence while still ill, complying with the doctor's treatment, not carrying out normal social roles and seeking help all fit the sick role. The sick role exempts the person from blame, so self-blame is the odd one out.

blocks.title: Disease vs illness vs sickness
rows: Actual pathology (e.g. a process that results in illness)
Personal experience (a set of symptoms suffered by a patient)

blocks.text: A man at work with headache, abdominal pain, dizziness, tiredness and fever is keyed as 'Illness' - the explanation says the description fits the illness itself rather than the patient's response or any social change. The distractors (health behaviour, sick role, abnormal illness behaviour, illness behaviour) all describe responses to illness, not the illness.
Health behaviours are seen in healthy people who try to maintain their health; they relate to primary prevention and are intended to reduce susceptibility to disease in the first place.

Mechanic and Volkart (1961) proposed illness behaviour: any behaviour by an individual who feels ill to relieve that experience or better define its meaning. It is an active process 'that involves interpreting symptoms, evaluating possible responses and, finally, deciding whether to try to alleviate those symptoms or simply to ignore them'.

Abnormal illness behaviour (Issy Pilowsky, 1969) extends this: persistence of a maladaptive mode of experiencing, perceiving, evaluating and responding to one's own health status despite a doctor having provided a lucid, accurate diagnosis and management plan with opportunities for discussion, negotiation and clarification, based on adequate bio-psycho-socio-cultural assessment.

Chest pain and dizziness with normal bloods and **ECG** is keyed as **ILLNESS** **BEHAVIOUR** - patients need not have a disease or disorder to show it and it can be abnormal; sick role, illness, depression and worried well are the distractors. A mock repeats the scenario with advice on medication, diet and exercise and keys illness behaviour again (behaviour by someone who feels ill to relieve or define the experience).

blocks.text: The International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities and Handicaps (**ICIDH**) provided a descriptive conceptual framework of the consequences of illnesses.

Health Beliefs Model (**HBM**): developed from the observation that patients have their own beliefs about disease risks and treatment benefits; patients' beliefs about their disease states may be more influential than medically determined disease information.

blocks.title: Health Beliefs Model: patient beliefs affecting treatment participation
rows: Susceptibility of acquiring the disease or its complications
Cost of treatment adherence (inconvenience, effort, time, money)
Environmental and social cues to action that may assist adherence

blocks.text: Transtheoretical Model (**TTM**; Prochaska and DiClemente, 1982) developed largely in response to increasing divergence in psychotherapy practice, as a (transtheoretical) synthesis among therapeutic systems; it identified five common processes of change for motivating individuals to change illness-related behaviours.

blocks.title: TTM: five processes of change
rows: Helping the patient gather information about self and the problem
Emotional expression of the problem behaviour and the process of change
Stimulus control (avoiding stimuli associated with the problem behaviour; operant extinction cueing effect) and counterconditioning (training an alternative, healthier response to the cue stimuli)
Positive reinforcement from others and self-appraisal, improving self-efficacy by self-reinforcement

blocks.title: Prochaska and DiClemente: six stages of change
rows: Not even considering changing; does not see the behaviour as a problem, minimizes and denies risks, avoids contrary information
Aware why the behaviour is a problem but ambivalent; likely sees equal or more benefits than costs
Has decided to change and is planning a strategy, but has not yet taken action
Has implemented a plan and is changing the behaviour
Has sustained the change and avoided reverting for a significant period of time
Reverts to problem behaviour, 'back to square one'

blocks.text: a man two weeks out of inpatient detoxification and abstaining was keyed 'Maintenance'. blocks.text: A patient willing to stop alcohol and accepting the need for change but who has taken no steps is keyed 'Ready for Action' in this mock; the explanation describes deciding and preparing to make a change (the preparation stage). The notes call this stage Preparation (decided to change and planning a strategy, not yet acted) - match the stem to the description, because the mock's label ('Ready for Action') is not the notes' stage name and Action means a plan already implemented.

The stages are not linear but cyclical (a person can relapse and re-enter at a later stage such as preparation); they do not operate in an invariant sequence (unlike Piaget's models); each stage can be moved into back and forth (reversibility); the stages are not qualitatively different.
Motivational Interviewing (Miller and Rollnick, 1991) is often used together with **TTM** and stages of change.

blocks.mnemonic: Please Consider Preparing: Act, Maintain, Relapse

bullets.text: ICIDH: impairment (structure/function), disability (whole-person activities), handicap (social disadvantage).
Health Beliefs Model: beliefs about severity, susceptibility, cost, benefit and cues to action drive treatment participation.
TTM (Prochaska and DiClemente 1982) has five processes of change: consciousness raising, choosing, catharsis, conditional stimuli, contingency control.
Six stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, relapse.
Stages are cyclical, reversible and not qualitatively different; Motivational Interviewing is often paired with TTM.

blocks.text: The General Medical Council (**UK**) and other professional organisations have set out the multitude of roles expected of a doctor; the RCPsych has adapted this to psychiatric practice.

blocks.caption: Diagram of six boxes, each with a heading and bullet: Doctors as scientists, health professionals, leaders, health advocates, teachers, health sector representatives.

blocks.title: Roles of the doctor (adapted by RCPsych)
rows: Accessing, interpreting and assimilating new knowledge critically
Listening and communicating appropriately, working as part of a team, non-judgmental behaviour, compassion and integrity
Day-to-day clinical decisions based on medical knowledge to assess impact, risk and likely outcome; skills in policy, strategy, service design and clinical processes
Critical decision makers responsible for allocation of significant health resources; influence to advocate for increased resources for patients and populations
Duty to contribute to the education of other professionals and patients, plus responsibility for continued personal education
Sharing responsibility to positively influence the culture and environment in which they work

blocks.text: Consensus Statement on the Role of the Doctor (medschools.ac.uk): doctors support patients in understanding their condition and what to expect (including when symptoms could have several causes); identify and advise on treatment options or preventive measures; and explain and discuss risks, benefits and uncertainties of tests and treatments, supporting patients to decide on their own care where possible.

All doctors have a role in maintaining and promoting population health through evidence-based practice; the doctor must appreciate the patient's needs in the context of the wider health needs of the population; for all doctors the patient must come first, achieved in different ways in different settings.

The social role of a psychiatrist includes being an appropriate role model giving effective support and guidance to those seeking treatment. Some leaders extend this to being a public figure and ambassador for the profession, educating the public via media to erase misperceptions about mental illness or psychiatry (Nasrallah, The model psychiatrist: 7 domains of excellence, 2011).

Professionalism: the American Board of Internal Medicine Foundation sets out three core principles, widely adopted by doctors in the **US**, **EU** and **UK**: primacy of patient welfare (dedication and altruism), patient autonomy, and social justice.

blocks.title: The 10 commitments to promote professionalism (Bhugra and Gupta, 2010)
rows: Maintaining trust by managing conflicts of interest
Professional responsibilities (including maximising patient care, self-regulation, remediation, disciplining)

blocks.text: Health advocacy is the process of supporting and empowering patients and carers to express their opinions, ideas and concerns, enabling them to access appropriate information and services and promoting their rights.

Dual loyalty (**WMA** Medical Ethics Manual): when physicians are accountable both to their patients and to a third party and these responsibilities are incompatible. Third parties include governments, employers (hospitals, managed healthcare organisations), insurers, military officials, police, prison officials and family members.

The **WMA** International Code states 'A physician shall owe his/her patients complete loyalty', yet it is generally accepted that physicians may in exceptional situations have to place the interests of others above those of the patient; the ethical challenge is deciding when and how to protect the patient against third-party pressures. One such situation is resource allocation.

Resource allocation: governments usually decide the overall healthcare budget and local bodies allocate it to services, but around ==80%== of healthcare expenditure distribution is controlled by end-providers. Where resources are limited all patients are entitled to a fair selection procedure; the **WMA** recommends the choice be based on medical criteria and made without discrimination.

blocks.title: Approaches to resource allocation
rows: Market principles (patient as consumer; willingness to pay)

**WMA** notes physicians have been gradually moving away from the traditional individualism of medical ethics, which would favour the libertarian approach, towards a more social conception of their role.

sections.title: 5. Family life in relation to major mental illnesses

blocks.text: The family is the most basic social unit and microcosm of an individual. The General Systems Model holds that families are systems where every action produces a reaction in one or more members; the system has external boundaries and internal rules, and every member plays a relatively stable but interchangeable role.

blocks.title: Family cycle
rows: Two individuals unite until the first child is born; tasks: forming a working dyad and restructuring relationships with families of origin
Birth of child to adolescence; major task: maintaining a satisfactory marital relationship amid the demands of childrearing
Children leave home; tasks: re-establishing individual interests and re-examining the marital relationship
Growth and extension of the family; task: maintaining ties across generations
Occurs due to decline or demise of partners

blocks.text: Family instability affects children depending on sex (boys more than girls), age (younger more than older) and temperament (hyperactive more than placid); it has a demonstrable effect on cognitive achievement, and the most common psychopathology noted is a behavioural difficulty. Family systems have been studied in detail with respect to schizophrenia especially.

blocks.title: Family theories of schizophrenia (all now disputed)
rows: Family in disequilibrium from repeated threats of parental separation; parents downgrade each other's roles and may collude with children and exclude partners
Equilibrium that is skewed and achieved at the expense of a distorted parental relationship; one parent dominant, the other submissive, making the marriage 'a stable fit'
Disjointed/fragmented communication patterns that may relate to later perceptual and thought disorders in schizophrenia

Superficial verbal communication contradicts behavioural and deeper communication, keeping the growing child in a double bind (cannot be correct either way), which can later increase the risk of psychosis
Mothers described as 'rejecting, impervious to the feelings of others, rigid in moralism concerning sex and had a significant fear of intimacy'

blocks.text: The schizophrenogenic mother was coined by Fromm-Reichmann - not Lidz, Rutter, Bateson or Wynne (the options that sound like the other family theorists). The explanation describes these mothers as rejecting, impervious to others' feelings, rigid about sex and fearful of intimacy, and adds that schizophrenogenic mother, marital skew and schism are now of historical interest only.

blocks.text: Contradictory parental demands that confuse the child and raise risk of emotional difficulty are keyed as the **DOUBLE** **BIND** (Bateson) - not marital schism (a Lidz term), learned helplessness, rapprochement or projective identification. The explanation describes a communication matrix in which messages contradict each other (primary, secondary and tertiary negative injunctions).

Lidz described these two 'schizophrenogenic' family patterns; Wynne and colleagues described communication patterns in which the child is forced to accept and develop a pattern of communication that negates and denies the existence of meaningless relationships in the family.

Causal links between these four family functions and schizophrenia are disputed and the models have fallen out of favour; there is no experimental evidence to support them and small data are poorly reproducible.

blocks.text: Expressed emotion (**EE**) was developed by Brown and Rutter in 1966 as part of the Camberwell Family Interview (**CFI**) and later modified by Vaughn and Leff in 1976; ratings were based on content and prosodic aspects and emphasis of speech.
The final scores of emotional over-involvement, critical comments and hostility were the most predictive measures for relapse of schizophrenia.

**CFI** is a long interview in which individual members of a family are interviewed (including the patient). If one relative is classified as high **EE**, the whole family could be classified as a high **EE** family. **CFI** ratings based on interviewing parents singly have the most predictive value.

**CFI** statement that is **NOT** true is 'carried out with the patient'. Notes vs bank disagree: the notes (p11) say individual family members are interviewed 'including the patient', while the **Q8** explanation says **CFI** involves interviewing family members 'not the patient'. The keyed answer follows the explanation's version.

blocks.text: The Five Minute Speech Sample (**FMSS**) was introduced as a substitute for **CFI** but tends to underestimate **EE**; it is more useful for measuring professional or staff carers' **EE**.

blocks.title: Relapse of schizophrenia by EE rating of the household (meta-analysis)

blocks.text: Worldwide the proportion of high **EE** in carers of patients with schizophrenia is ==52%==, with the lowest rates in India and other developing nations; the strength of association between relapse and **EE** is identical for both genders.

In a majority of studies high **EE** predicted relapse of schizophrenia symptoms 9 months later for both genders. More than 35 hours per week of face-to-face contact with a high **EE** relative increased relapse risk, but in low **EE** households high contact appeared protective.

Reducing face-to-face contact with a high-**EE** family may reduce relapse is the **TRUE** statement: more than 35 hours per week of contact with a high-**EE** relative raises relapse risk, but with low-**EE** households high contact appeared protective. High **EE** is not claimed as the cause of schizophrenia, does not cause poor insight, is **NOT** measured by the Camberwell Assessment of Needs, and predicts relapse in both genders (the distractors).

Other-initiated separation or a rift in a close tie, probably permanent or long-term, or 'forced' by circumstances (e.g. the subject's infidelity, marked violence); delinquent behaviour of a child or criminal act by a close tie; 'put down' events such as rejection or verbal/physical attack by a close tie or publicly by anyone (includes all rapes)

Long-term sustained entrapment (serious difficulties that can only get worse or persist, per the subject) or a failed positive event where a potential fresh start went disastrously wrong within 1-2 weeks, leaving the person stuck in 'square one'

blocks.text: A unidimensional measure of severity (loss or threat, etc.) is not sufficient to explain effects on mental illness. blocks.title: Kendler et al. (2003): which event type predicts which onset

blocks.text: Humiliation is the keyed life-event type that predicts onset of **PURE** depressive illness (Kendler et al. 2003) - not loss, threat, danger or entrapment. The explanation: humiliation predicted pure major depression but not pure generalised anxiety, danger predicted pure generalised anxiety but not pure major depression, and combined loss and humiliation events are more depressogenic than threat; the results had only moderate predictive strength.

Depressed patients may recall more stressful life events due to cognitive bias. The frequency of desirable ('entrance') life events in depressed people is comparable to controls, so absence of positive events cannot be the simple explanation for depression. Recurrent depressive episodes have fewer preceding life events than a first episode, which may relate to kindling.

'His depression is probably due to absence of positive life events' is the **INCORRECT** explanation - the explanation says desirable (entrance) events were comparable in controls and the depressed, so absence of positive events cannot be the simple explanation. sections.title: 8. Social causation, social drift and poverty

blocks.text: Engel's biopsychosocial model is widely used in aetiological formulations in psychiatric practice, highlighting the prominence of social factors.

blocks.title: Social causation vs social drift
rows: Mental illnesses are caused by social deprivation; most psychiatric disorders are seen in lower socio-economic class as a direct result of poverty and social conditions
Illness (e.g. schizophrenia) results in downward drift of economic status rather than poverty causing it
May hold for depression or alcohol misuse, but not bipolar disorder or schizophrenia
Suggested by the schizophrenia survey data (patients' fathers' class matched the general population)
First suggested by Faris and Dunham, 'Chicago study 1922-1934'

blocks.text: Survey of males aged 25-34 on first admission with schizophrenia: an expected excess of social class V was noted, but the social class distribution of the patients' fathers was the same as the general population - suggesting schizophrenia causes downward drift rather than poverty causing it.

Faris and Dunham applied the concentric zone model of urban organisation: social organisation increased with distance from the epicentre (inner urban zones = most disorganised and unstable; outer zones = most organised and stable). The least socially organised inner zones had the highest schizophrenia rates, which they argued was due to downward drift after developing the illness.

blocks.caption: Concentric zone model of urban organisation (Chicago), labelled URBAN AREAS: zones I Loop, II Zone in transition, III Zone of workingmen's homes, IV Residential zone, V Commuters zone, with areas such as Single family dwellings, Residential hotels, Bright light area, Black belt, Deutschland, Ghetto, Two flat area, Restricted residential district, Bungalow section.

blocks.text: Factors mediating the effect of social class include lower educational levels, poverty, immigration, overcrowding, poorer physical health and nutrition. For **ADHD**, high parental education is associated with lower risk (especially in boys); there is no proven link with food additives, but lead exposure is associated with risk.

Pregnancy and birth factors associated with **ADHD**, increasing its prevalence among lower social classes: toxaemia or eclampsia, poor maternal health, maternal age, foetal post-maturity, long labour, foetal distress, antepartum haemorrhage, low birth weight and prematurity.

Food additives are keyed as **NOT** a risk factor for **ADHD** - the explanation says there is no proven link; **ADHD** and its common complications are associated with low social class, large family size, paternal antisocial personality and maternal mental disorder (large family size, family history, low birth weight and low parental education are the other options).

blocks.title: Rutter: six inter-related family risk factors for childhood mental disturbance

blocks.mnemonic: Some Lazy Lions Mostly Prowl Free

blocks.text: Rutter observed that the aggregate of these adverse factors, rather than any one factor, impaired development.

Poverty and psychopathology (Great Smoky Mountains study): children were grouped as 'poor', 'never-poor' and 'ex-poor' (ex-poor families whose income rose when a casino was built on American Indian land). Before the casino opened, poor and ex-poor children had more psychiatric problems; afterwards the ex-poor fell to the never-poor level. The issues most responsive to poverty were conduct and oppositional defiant disorders, while depression and anxiety prevalence stayed the same.

sections.title: 9. Sociology of mental illness: deviance and labelling

blocks.text: Mental illness as deviance: society tends to see odd and abnormal behaviour as against acceptable norms and values, and some of this is grouped as mental illness; deviance becomes an important determinant of the illness concept. Edwin Lemert developed primary and secondary deviance to explain labelling.

blocks.title: Primary vs secondary deviance (Lemert)
rows: Any general aberration from expected normality before the person is identified as 'deviant'
Actions carried out by a person identified as 'deviant' by institutions (society, justice system)
Minor rule breaking such as over-speeding
With repeated primary deviance the subject is labelled and institutions react; secondary deviance is the maintenance of primary deviance as a repercussion of the label

blocks.text: Suspiciousness that worsens after colleagues avoid a man following a schizophrenia diagnosis is **SECONDARY** deviance (a response to the label), not primary deviance - the explanation reserves primary deviance for the symptoms themselves (hallucinations, thought disorder); partial, formal and spiral deviance are distractors. Labelling theory is Lemert's, developed by Scheff, and a label can function as a self-fulfilling prophecy.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PSYCHOLOGY/9) Sociocultural Psychiatry Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Societal reaction thus initiates sociological/psychological processes that sustain deviance, making it more central to the life of the 'deviant'.

blocks.title: Formal vs informal deviance
rows: Breaking a written law or code of constitution, as in a criminal act
Breaking unspoken social rules of living

blocks.text: Deviancy amplification spiral (originally applied to crime reporting): it starts with a 'deviant' act; media report it as newsworthy and add similar non-newsworthy items ('sensationalism'), setting up bias so that minor problems look serious and rare events seem common; mounting public concern follows, forcing law enforcement to focus more resources on the deviancy than it warrants.

Social construction theory explores how variations in human experience have come to be classed as illness categories, using 'deconstruction' or discourse analysis; the reality of mental illness is socially constructed and complicated by the cognitive interests of social groups - doctors, lawmakers, politicians.

blocks.title: Examples offered for social construction
rows: Agoraphobia developed as a concept around the time of the social emancipation of women, so might partly originate from problematised use of public space
Sexual role stereotypes may play a role in anxiety disorder constructs and psychopathy

Most major mental problems are circularly defined (a patient is termed 'psychotic' because he hears a voice, and is told he hears a voice because he is psychotic); most labels are circular descriptions constructed by society

blocks.text: Social labelling (societal reaction) theory originated from symbolic interactionism: each person plays many socially sanctioned roles and the meaning of interactions depends on the role assumed. Thomas Scheff (Being Mentally Ill, 1966) expanded labelling theory to mental illness.

Scheff: social routine is made of numerous uncategorisable, unspoken, taken-for-granted residual rules. Residual deviance occurs when these are broken; rule breaking is accepted, ignored or normalised in some circumstances but labelled deviant in others.

Labelling may occur in one-off crises or as a gradual shift from acceptance to labelling, depending on the effect of the deviance on others. This might explain why many voice hearers live in the community without a schizophrenia diagnosis and why community surveys always show higher prevalence than clinical samples.

Once labelled mentally ill, the person takes up the role of a mentally ill individual, which sanctions certain privileges as compensation for loss of others; self-labelling strengthens beliefs about the role. Original labelling theory is empirical without much experimental support; a modified labelling theory is now used to explain the effect of stigma on relapses.

bullets.text: Primary deviance = aberration before being labelled; secondary deviance = maintaining it as a repercussion of the institutional label (Lemert).
Formal deviance breaks written law; informal deviance breaks unspoken social rules.
Deviancy amplification spiral: media sensationalism, public concern, over-focus by law enforcement.
Social construction: illness categories are socially constructed (agoraphobia, circular definitions) via discourse analysis.
Scheff: residual rules and residual deviance; labelling can be sudden or gradual; labelled person takes the sick role identity.

blocks.text: Durkheim, often called the father of sociology, described a sociological model of suicide with 4 types; both an unusually 'tight' bondage and weak adherence to societal values can contribute to suicide (altruistic and anomic respectively).

Excessive individualism but low social integration; no cohesive group attachment
Society's control on the individual is so strong that it interferes with moral values and personal goals
Individual feels no guidance or regulation from the societal system; feels disillusioned

sections.title: 11. Social factors in schizophrenia: urbanicity, migration and ethnicity

blocks.text: Significant social disadvantage (racism, discrimination, economic and employment disadvantage, perceived 'outsider status') is evident in populations at higher risk of schizophrenia. Social defeat hypothesis: long-term social disadvantage leads to sensitisation of the dopamine system and/or increased baseline activity, thus increased schizophrenia risk; immigrant populations exemplify the link.

Social adversity brings a high degree of stress that can be exceptionally harmful in vulnerability to psychosis (shown in many animal studies). Child abuse is not seen as a specific risk factor for schizophrenia but may be a marker for relevant factors such as family dysfunction.

Neighbourhood effect: in neighbourhoods with ethnic minorities (non-white) at increased risk, the risk reduced when the minority population increased; natives had increased risk where minorities were more numerous - supporting social adversity as a risk factor.

blocks.title: Urban effect on psychosis
rows: Children born in urban environments are at increased risk for psychosis in most parts of the globe (**OR** 1.61; **CI** 1.4-1.8)
Not consistent across all countries; some Australian research found no increase in urban areas
Marcelis et al. (1998, Dutch National Psychiatric Register): effect of urbanicity on all psychosis greater for men than women
Urban-birth effect greatest in the most recent birth cohorts and with early-onset disease, even after correcting for follow-up length
Positive correlation between schizophrenia admission rates and degree of urbanisation
Consistent dose-response between urbanicity and schizophrenia risk: the larger the town of birth, the greater the risk

blocks.text: Being born in an urban area is the keyed factor most associated with increased schizophrenia risk - not frequently being placed in a double-bind situation, high expressed emotion in the family home, or maternal cannabis or alcohol use in pregnancy. The explanation calls the evidence robust and consistent (McGrath 2006), matching the notes' dose-response urban-birth findings.

Immigration and schizophrenia: although most mental illnesses are more frequent in migrants than natives, schizophrenia has been studied most; Cooper reappraised the data and summarised the main findings below.

blocks.title: Cooper's findings on immigration and schizophrenia
rows: Excess risk is not specific to African-Caribbean immigrants; also in African-born Black immigrants to the **UK** and, to a lesser extent, Asian immigrants - so any explanation cannot be purely biological or simply race specific

Incidence in Caribbean countries is similar to the indigenous **UK** population, excluding the country-of-origin theory; rates are higher in **UK**-born second-generation African-Caribbeans than in the first generation, strongly suggesting an environmental rather than genetic effect

No evidence of selective immigration from the Caribbean; second-generation children of immigrants also have very high psychosis rates (sometimes higher than parents), negating psychosis-induced immigration

Long delays in seeking help, lower likelihood of psychiatric referral, frequent police/emergency service involvement, high proportions of compulsory, intensive care and secure ward admissions; long-term outcome correspondingly unfavourable

blocks.text: for a young Jamaican immigrant with schizophrenia, the keyed statement is that the risk in his parents is similar to the risk in native patients' parents (prepsychotic segregation does not explain it; social adversity is the more acceptable notion).

blocks.text: Being a migrant is keyed as the risk factor most highly associated with schizophrenia in a young man - over early loss of the mother, living alone, alcohol use and **HLA-DR2**. The explanation: rates are increased in first- and second-generation migrants, this cannot be attributed to high incidence in their countries of origin, and host-country stress factors (exclusion, discrimination, defeat) contribute.

blocks.text: Goffman described a 'total institution' as one 'whose character is symbolized by the barrier to social intercourse with the outside'.

blocks.title: Characteristics of total institutions (Goffman)
rows: All aspects of life conducted in the same premises under the same unitary authority
Each member's daily activities carried on in immediate proximity of a large batch of others required to do the same
All parts of a day's activities strictly scheduled, one leading into the next
The different enforced activities are based on a single plan fulfilling the institution's official (statutory) aims

blocks.text: Goffman's 'moral career' of a mentally ill patient: the process whereby a person with social ties, friends and family in the community is institutionalised and converted into an inmate whose world is limited to the hospital ambience (Peele et al. 1977).

blocks.caption: Four-step arrow diagram: Step 1 Betrayal funnel; Step 2 Role stripping; Step 3 Mortification; Step 4 Privilege system, each with its printed explanation.

blocks.title: Goffman's moral career: four steps
rows: The people we trust most (family, friends) conspire against us when unwell, reporting our actions to doctors and mental health professionals (the 'circuit of agents') who run the decision-making
Institutionalisation begins with a series of assaults on the recruit's self; stripping of identity through rituals such as trading personal clothes and belongings for hospital issue

A series of assaults on self-image; at the end one becomes a 'full member'. Private activities go on public display and permission is needed for minor volitional acts (smoking, shaving, toilet) - termed 'civil death'
The patient is inserted into the lowest rung of an all-embracing privilege system based on house rules; privileges are reductions in the institution's control; freedom is a token of reward

blocks.text: Family and friends reporting a patient's actions to professionals to get him admitted is Goffman's **BETRAYAL** **FUNNEL**, the first step of the moral career - not role stripping, batch living, mortification or institutional neurosis (the later steps/other terms). A mock repeats this item and its explanation says that at each stage of admission family and friends may give the impression the patient will not lose any more of his rights.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PSYCHOLOGY/9) Sociocultural Psychiatry Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: According to Goffman, stripping and the privilege system are offered as being in the patient's best interests and on therapeutic grounds, but their real purpose is to break his spirit and make him more manageable; they introduce him to a therapeutic milieu and a new 'patient identity'.

blocks.title: Batch living vs binary living
rows: All inmates do 'the same thing' and lead a very similar life inside the institution
Staff lives contrast starkly: staff have power and connection with the outside world and can change their lives; a binary division exists between staff and inmates

blocks.text: Goffman considered 'secondary adjustments' a direct result of institutionalisation and a hallmark of institutionalism: habitual arrangements by which patients act as if their major concern is to escape the institution's pervasive control, usually unauthorised activities obtaining unauthorised ends.

Russell Barton (1976) described 'institutional neurosis': apathy, lack of initiative, loss of interest and submissiveness. Proposed causes: loss of contact with the outside world, enforced idleness, brutality and authoritativeness of staff, loss of friends and possessions, poor ward atmosphere and loss of prospects outside.

Institutional neurosis was described by Russell Barton (1976) - not Goffman, Parsons, Pavlov or Pilowsky (Goffman is one of the options but is not keyed). Barton's features: apathy, lack of initiative, loss of interest and submissiveness, attributed to loss of contact with the outside world, enforced idleness and staff bossiness.

blocks.text: Social reactivity and schizophrenia: Wing and Brown surveyed asylums (Mapperley, Netherne, Severalls) in the late fifties and concluded social poverty and lack of stimulation were related to the severity of blunted affect, poverty of speech and social withdrawal ('clinical poverty'); the relationship was weak in a 1990 reappraisal (Curson et al., 1992). Too much stimulation could provoke positive symptoms.

Morgan (1979) coined malignant alienation: progressive deterioration in the relationship between carers (ward staff) and a patient, with loss of sympathy and support; staff construe behaviour as provocative, unreasonable or overdependent. It may precede suicide or attempted suicide.

Nurses angry that a newly admitted patient 'splits them' with conflicting messages at ward rounds are describing **MALIGNANT** **ALIENATION** (Morgan 1979) - not introjection, identification, elimination or transference. The explanation: progressive deterioration in the relationship between staff and patient with loss of sympathy and support, behaviour construed as provocative, unreasonable or overdependent, sometimes preceding suicide or attempted suicide.

The notes give the barrier-to-social-intercourse definition but not the 1961/Asylums attribution.

blocks.text: Criminology is the study of crime, its origin and effects.

blocks.title: Broader scope of criminology
rows: Effects of crime on victims and society

blocks.title: Three levels of explanation of criminal behaviour

blocks.text: Different criminology theories construct their primary explanation at one of these levels.

Penology (Latin poena, punishment) deals with the societal response to and treatment of crime and criminals and focuses on the workings of the Criminal Justice System; its broad goal is to aid society to repress criminality. In mental health contexts it also covers medical treatment and education aimed at rehabilitation and social inclusion of the offender.

Crime and mental health: the relationship is hard to establish. Crime is defined in a social context (what is a crime varies by time and place), convictions are not the same as crimes and most data are on convictions, and it is hard to tell whether mental illness was directly related to an offence.

bullets.text: Criminology studies criminal attributes, extent of crime, effects on victims/society, prevention and types.
Three explanatory levels: individual, situational/contextual, social-structural.
Penology (poena = punishment): societal response to crime; in mental health also treatment and rehabilitation.
Crime-mental health link is hard to study: crime is socially defined, convictions differ from crimes, causation is unanswerable.

blocks.text: Stigma (Goffman) is an attribute, trait or behaviour considered shameful that symbolically marks the possessor as unacceptable, inferior or dangerous.

blocks.caption: Shaded table headed STIGMA TYPES: enacted, felt, public, self- and courtesy stigma with definitions.

blocks.title: Types of stigma

blocks.text: **NIMBY** (Not In My Back Yard) opposition: vehement disapproval by local authorities and social groups of siting a community mental health facility in an area, due to fear and stigma. A Mind survey found more than two-thirds of mental health services in England and Wales faced such opposition; main concerns were children's safety, falling house prices and violence.

blocks.text: 'Cost of treatment required' is the item that is **NOT** a Hayward and Bright theme behind stigma against mental illness - the four are dangerousness, attribution of responsibility (blaming), poor prognosis and disruption of social interaction; blaming, poor prognosis, disruption and dangerousness appear as the distractors.

blocks.text: These four themes formed the basis of an Office of National Statistics survey of **UK** public attitudes: schizophrenia and addictions were regarded most negatively; about ==60%== thought addicted individuals have only themselves to blame; most knew differences between disorders and felt depression and anxiety are treatable. Little changed over 10 years: over ==80%== endorsed 'most people are embarrassed by mentally ill people' and about ==30%== agreed 'I am embarrassed by mentally ill persons' (Huxley, 1993).

Surveys with case vignettes (Jorm et al., 1997): professionals rate antidepressants (depression) and antipsychotics plus admission (schizophrenia) as much more helpful than the public; the public rate vitamins/minerals and special diets (both disorders) and self-help books (schizophrenia) much more favourably; practitioners' beliefs about mental disorders differ greatly from the public's.

blocks.title: Hagighat's unifying theory: stigma serves stigmatisers' self-interest
rows: Quick and easy stereotypes at the expense of depth; the brain weights negative evaluations preferentially; repeated violence by a few is read as violence by 'the mentally ill'; links rare negative events with rare objects such as minority groups
Using the 'unfortunate other' to feel happier about oneself; those with low self-esteem derogate others to bolster it
Stigmatising rivals as a weapon in socio-economic competition; more intense in more competitive, self-seeking societies
Stigmatisation may have an evolutionary advantage, e.g. avoiding discriminated people as mates

blocks.title: How stigma evolves (Link and Phelan, 2001)
rows: People distinguish and label human differences
Dominant cultural beliefs link labelled persons to undesirable characteristics (negative stereotypes)
Labelled persons are placed in distinct categories - 'us' vs 'them'

blocks.text: Corrigan distinguishes three stigma components: stereotypes (e.g. schizophrenics are violent), prejudice (endorsing negative stereotypes, giving emotional reactions) and discrimination (the resulting behavioural reaction).

blocks.title: Dimensions of stigma (Jones et al., 2000)
rows: How obvious/detectable; less concealable problems are more stigmatised
Whether reversible over time; irreversible conditions elicit more negative attitudes
Extent to which it strains interpersonal interactions; stigma is directly proportional to the disruption produced
Attractiveness; a disorder eliciting disgust is more stigmatised
Understanding of cause; a condition thought self-inflicted has higher stigma
Feelings of danger or threat; highly threatening problems are highly stigmatised

blocks.title: MIND's three types of antistigma intervention (after NIMBY survey)
rows: Popularising how common mental illness is (e.g. the '==1 in 4==' film from Changing Minds), improving contact between mentally ill people and neighbours

blocks.text: Legislative intervention: little experimental evidence on anti-discrimination legislation; it may reduce discriminatory acts but not prejudice or stereotypes, may increase debate and self-questioning, and people may change behaviour to avoid sanctions; but suppressed discrimination may reappear in subtle, unpunishable forms - it may suppress but not eliminate stigma.

Affective intervention (e.g. contact between neighbourhood and hostel residents): generalising from a few hostel inmates to all mentally ill people cannot be drawn; neighbours' mobility was higher than in a control street; risk of reinforcing stereotypes by sub-typing better ones from the 'dangerous' ones.
Public education has had mixed results: focussed interventions can increase socially desirable responses in post-campaign surveys but not improve behaviour; ignorance is not the only cause of stigma.

blocks.title: Liz Sayce: four models for addressing stigma and social exclusion
rows: An illness like any other; danger of lacking credibility, too paternalistic, may make the ill person 'a victim of fate'
A continuum/spectrum of mental health and illness (dimensional); critiqued as advocating the status quo rather than attitude/cultural change, though popular in mental health promotion
Equal rights and equal criminal responsibility for service users; biggest concern is a net series of losses in courts and workplace
The favoured approach: social inclusion on civil rights grounds, not paternalistic help; disability = impairment plus socially imposed barriers and prejudices

blocks.text: The stigma-reduction model that demands equal rights and equal criminal responsibility for the mentally ill is the **LIBERTARIAN** model - not the brain-disease/no-fault model, individual growth model or disability inclusion model. The explanation says it advocates equal rights without discrimination, positive or negative, with the risk of serial losses for the mentally ill at work or in court.

Changing Minds was a 5-year campaign led by Kendell and colleagues at the Royal College of Psychiatrists. In the RCPsych 1998 survey, ==70%== believed people with schizophrenia are violent and unpredictable. '==1 in 4==' is a short 2-minute film for 15-25 year olds; 'Every Family in the Land' is a book on stigma; other methods included tube cards, press articles, videos and road shows.

Labelling and stigma (Angermeyer et al. 2003, nearly 5000 German nationals): labelling as mental illness affects public attitudes to people with schizophrenia - endorsing the dangerousness stereotype strongly raises preference for social distance; perceiving a need for help evokes mixed feelings and moves desire for social distance both ways; labelling has practically no effect on attitudes to major depression.

Normalisation (from the deinstitutionalisation of people with developmental disabilities) is providing life in 'normalized' community settings, using means as culturally normative as possible (Wolfensberger 1972). Social role valorisation (Wolfensberger, 1983) expands it: creating and defending valued social roles for devalued people, in response to the universal phenomenon of social devaluation.

Emic perspective: that of an individual from a specific cultural group about their own group. Etic perspective: that of an individual outside the group; the etic approach for instance applies Western psychiatric concepts en bloc to another culture for diagnosis.

blocks.text: Acculturation is the cultural change when an individual or group comes into continuous contact with a culturally distinct group; it can result from immigration and can occur in either direction (hosts can become acculturated, e.g. in colonial rule). Berry's model describes four types by retention and adoption of the two cultures at ethnocultural group level.

blocks.text: Integration: high retention of own values and high adoption of the new culture. Separation: high retention and low adoption. Marginalisation: low retention and low adoption; these individuals are marginalised by both the culture of origin and the culture of adoption. Assimilation is described as partial adaptation of a new culture (seen in migrants or refugees) without retaining or giving up all of one's culture of origin completely. blocks.text: The therapist's view of the patient's cultural identity is the keyed **EXCEPTION** in cultural formulation - the patient's own view of his cultural identity matters more. The other options are included: cultural elements in the patient-therapist relationship, cultural explanations of distress, influence of the psychosocial environment, and diagnosis in the context of the patient's cultural background.

Explanatory models are not fixed: they are influenced by circumstances of the symptoms, age, gender, educational attainment, time point and context of assessment and, importantly, cultural beliefs; they can themselves influence a physician's assessments. Exploring the patient's identity and explanatory model improves understanding and helps negotiate different worldviews, without requiring the psychiatrist to enter another culture as a participant observer.

Age, gender, cultural background, time and context of assessment and educational status all influence a patient's explanatory (health belief) model - 'a history of good physical health' is the keyed **EXCEPTION**. The explanation credits Kleinman's work with showing the importance of the patient's understanding of the cause of illness when treating it.

Idioms of distress: idioms are well-structured, codified ways of expressing thoughts through language that lose meaning when translated out of context; in cultural psychiatry they are somatic symptoms that serve as a code for expressing mental distress in some cultures.

Following both prescribed medication and ethnic/spiritual therapy may best secure adherence; encourages honest discussion with family and maintaining religious affiliations

blocks.text: Culture-bound syndromes are identified in both **ICD** and **DSM**. Most are locally flavoured varieties of illnesses found elsewhere, and most actually occur in many unrelated cultures. The explanatory mechanisms (e.g. witchcraft, humoral imbalances) are the defining features more than the symptom profiles.

Such illness beliefs can lead to behaviours that seem to indicate disordered thought outside their cultural context but make sense within it (example in the notes: the Chinese syndromes pa-feng and pa-leng).

blocks.text: 'Mind is a bodily organ and can be diseased' is the keyed statement that is **NOT** a central anti-psychiatry belief - anti-psychiatry holds that medication and hospitalisation are harmful, the scientific method cannot explain subjective abnormality, mental disorder is explained by social factors, and labelling someone 'ill' is an artificial device. Szasz wrote The Myth of Mental Illness (his question: 'Is there such a thing as mental illness?').
Phenomenology is a method to define more clearly the subjective essence of a given experience, reducing broad human experience to a simpler subject matter (Broome, 2007).

Karl Jaspers laid the foundation for today's descriptive psychopathology, introduced phenomenology to psychiatry, and distinguished causal explanation (aetiology) from meaningful understanding (description); Ghaemi (2007) regards this as the first scientific foundation to psychiatry.

blocks.title: Jaspers: understanding vs explanation
rows: Psychological intuition about the meaning of a psychological state or event for another individual
Observable influence of one event or process on another that can be tested objectively

blocks.text: Psychiatry requires both understanding and explanation.

Descriptive psychopathology does not attempt to explain causality but restricts itself to 'understanding' experience by describing what is observed, requiring a common terminology. It has two components: observation of behaviour, plus empathic assessment of subjective experience (which Jaspers calls phenomenology).
Empathy ('feeling like how your patient might feel') differs from sympathy (feeling sorry or pitiful for the patient); empathy is essential for learning about pathological processes.

blocks.text: The Nuremberg Code was the code of ethics following the Nuremberg Trials (post-World War **II** trial concerning doctors experimenting on people detained in concentration camps).
